docs.title: AlgoStudio Teacher Docs
docs.text:
Welcome! This is the guide for teachers using AlgoStudio.

Here you'll learn how to set up problems, write test cases, and check what your students are doing.

docs.title: What you can do right now
docs.text:
• Create problems with test cases, descriptions, and starter code
  • Edit problem files through the browser
  • See every submission a student has made, including what changed between attempts

docs.title: What's coming
docs.text:
• Creating courses through the UI
  • Assigning problems to courses through the UI
  • Student enrollment and management

docs.title: Quick links
docs.text:
• Getting started
  • Making a problem
  • Viewing student work

docs.title: Log in
docs.text: Go to your AlgoStudio URL and click Log in with GitHub. You need a GitHub account. If you don't have one, make one at github.com — it's free.

docs.title: Find a problem
docs.text:
Once you're logged in, go to /p/<problem-id> to open a problem. The ID comes from whoever set up the server.

Creating problems through the UI is coming soon

Right now, problems have to be created directly in the database. Once the UI is ready, you'll be able to create them from the browser.

docs.title: Edit a problem
docs.text:
If you have access, go to /p/<problem-id>/manage to manage a problem's files. From there you can:

  • Edit the description
  • Edit the test cases
  • Edit the starter code
  • Add or remove files

See the Problems section to learn what each file does.

docs.title: Courses
docs.text:
Courses are groups of problems. You can use them to organise problems by topic, week, or class.

Course management through the UI is coming soon

Courses currently have to be created directly in the database. The UI for creating and managing courses isn't built yet.

Once it's ready, you'll be able to:

  • Create a course with a name and icon
  • Add problems to a course
  • Share a course link with students

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
A problem is made up of files. Each file has a specific job. You manage them at /p/<problem-id>/manage.

File What it does expectedOutputs.json The test cases — what inputs to try and what answers to expect readme.md The problem description shown to students .placeholder The starter code shown when a student first opens the problem

All three files are optional, but a problem without expectedOutputs.json can't be tested.

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text:
• Test cases — how to write expectedOutputs.json
  • Problem description — how to write readme.md
  • Placeholder code — how to write .placeholder
  • Editing files — how to use the file editor

docs.title: Problem Description
docs.text: The file readme.md is the description students read when they open the problem. It's shown next to the code editor.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
Write it in Markdown. If you don't know Markdown, here's the basics:

# Big heading

## Smaller heading

Normal paragraph text.

- Bullet point
- Another bullet point

**Bold text** and _italic text_.

`code like this`

    code block
    (indent with 4 spaces)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# Add Two Numbers

Write a function called `add` that takes two numbers and returns their sum.

## Example

add(1, 2)  → 3
add(5, 5)  → 10

## Rules

- You cannot use any libraries
- Your function must be named exactly `add`

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Keep it short. Students are there to code, not read.
  • Show an example or two. It's easier than explaining in words.
  • Tell students exactly what the function should be named.

docs.title: Editing Files
docs.text: Go to /p/<problem-id>/manage to see all the files on a problem.

docs.title: Opening a file
docs.text: Click a file to open it in the editor. Make your changes and save.

docs.title: Adding a file
docs.text: Use the New File button to add a file. Give it a name — for example readme.md or expectedOutputs.json.

docs.title: Renaming a file
docs.text: Right-click a file in the manage view to rename it.

docs.title: Deleting a file
docs.text:
Right-click a file in the manage view to delete it.

Warning

Deleting expectedOutputs.json means the problem can no longer be tested until you add it back.

docs.title: Placeholder Code
docs.text: The file .placeholder is the starter code students see when they first open the problem. It appears in the editor automatically.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
For a problem where students write a function called add:

def add(a, b):
    # write your solution here
    pass

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Always include the function signature. Students shouldn't have to guess the name or parameters.
  • The function name must exactly match the functionName set on the problem — that's what the test runner looks for.
  • Keep it minimal. Don't give away the solution.

Note

If .placeholder doesn't exist, the editor starts empty.

docs.title: Test Cases
docs.text: Test cases live in a file called expectedOutputs.json. This file tells AlgoStudio what inputs to give the student's function and what the correct answer should be.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
The file is a list. Each item is a pair: the inputs, and the expected output.

[
  [[1, 2], 3],
  [[10, 20], 30],
  [[-1, 1], 0]
]

Each item looks like this: [[inputs], expected_output]

  • The inputs are always a list, even if there's only one
  • The expected output is whatever the function should return

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Say you have a problem where students write a function called add that adds two numbers.

[
  [[1, 2], 3],
  [[5, 5], 10],
  [[-1, 1], 0],
  [[0, 0], 0]
]

When a student submits, AlgoStudio runs add(1, 2) and checks if the answer is 3, then add(5, 5) and checks for 10, and so on.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• More test cases = better feedback. Students see which ones passed and which ones failed.
  • Include edge cases. Zeros, negatives, empty inputs — these are where bugs hide.
  • The function name matters. The problem has a functionName set when it was created. Your test cases must match that function.

The file must be valid JSON

If expectedOutputs.json has a syntax error, the problem won't run. Use a JSON validator if you're unsure.

docs.title: Viewing Student Submissions
docs.text: You can see every submission a student has made for a problem.

docs.title: How to get there
docs.text:
Go to /p/<problem-id>/users/<user-id>.

You'll see a list of all their submissions in order, including:

  • The code they submitted
  • Which test cases passed and which failed
  • The output and expected output for each test case
  • How long each test case took to run

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
• Progression — did they get closer over time, or are they stuck?
  • Wrong output — what is their function returning vs what was expected?
  • Errors — is it crashing? The error message will show under the test case.

Finding a student's user ID

Student user IDs are not yet shown in a teacher dashboard. You'll need to look them up in the database directly for now. A student list UI is coming soon.
